questions.stem: Changing only the temperature of a reaction affects

options.text: The rate constant k, which then changes value
options.explanation: k is fixed only at constant temperature, so heating re-values it.
Both respond to temperature in Arrhenius terms.

options.text: The orders m and n in the rate equation
options.explanation: Orders are temperature-independent kinetic facts.

options.text: Only the rate, leaving k untouched
options.explanation: Rate and k move together through the energetic fraction.

questions.stem: Raising the temperature increases the rate because

options.text: The concentration of reactants increases on heating
options.explanation: Heating does not create extra reactant.

options.text: A greater proportion of molecules then carry energy at or above the activation energy
options.explanation: The energetic fraction grows exponentially with T.

options.text: The activation energy itself falls when mixtures are heated
options.explanation: Ea is a reaction constant; heating does not move the barrier.

options.text: Molecules collide less often but hit harder
options.explanation: Collision frequency rises too, but the decisive factor is the energetic fraction.

questions.stem: In the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(-Ea/RT), the term A represents

options.text: The gas constant shared by every reaction
options.explanation: That is R.
Concentrations belong to the rate equation, not here.

options.text: The Arrhenius constant, characteristic of the particular reaction
options.explanation: A is the reaction's own pre-exponential constant.

options.text: The activation energy of the reaction
options.explanation: That is Ea.

questions.stem: Which quantities act as the only variables in the Arrhenius equation?

options.explanation: Both are characteristic constants of the reaction.
R is universal and Ea is fixed per reaction.
Ea does not vary with conditions in this treatment.
Ea, A and R are constants; only k and T change.

questions.stem: A catalyst is swapped for a different one in a running reaction. The value of k

options.text: Changes, because altering the catalyst is a condition change that k responds to
options.explanation: The Arrhenius picture treats catalyst identity as a condition that re-values k.

options.text: Stays the same, because k only cares about temperature
options.explanation: Concentration is not the only variable that matters; catalyst changes count too.
Catalysis never drives k to zero.
Rate constants are positive quantities.

questions.stem: State the Arrhenius equation and identify the constants in it.
questions.modelAnswer: k = A e^(-Ea/RT), where Ea and A are constants characteristic of the reaction, R is the universal gas constant, and k and T are the variables.

questions.stem: State what happens to the rate constant when temperature is raised, and why.
questions.modelAnswer: The rate constant increases, because a greater proportion of molecules then hold energy at least equal to the activation energy, and k is proportional to that energetic fraction.

questions.stem: Explain why raising the temperature raises the rate constant k.
questions.modelAnswer: The rate constant is proportional to the fraction of molecules holding at least the activation energy; distributing molecular energies more widely at higher temperature enlarges that fraction, so k must rise with T.

questions.stem: Two identical reactions run at 300 K and 320 K with the same Ea and A. Which run shows the larger k, and what does that predict for the observed rate?
questions.modelAnswer: The 320 K run has the larger k because the exponential energetic fraction grows with T; since rate is proportional to k at fixed concentrations, the warmer mixture reacts measurably faster.

questions.stem: Taking natural logarithms of the Arrhenius equation gives

options.explanation: ln A keeps its positive sign.
The exponential rearranges into a straight-line log form.
The minus sign survives: the Ea term enters negatively.
Only the logarithm of k appears on the left.

questions.stem: Increasing the activation energy Ea, at fixed temperature, makes k

options.text: Unchanged, since Ea only affects the rate
options.explanation: k and the rate move together; both fall.
k stays positive regardless.

options.text: Smaller, because fewer molecules then reach the energetic bar
options.explanation: The exponential term shrinks as Ea grows.
Collision count is not the Ea effect here.

questions.stem: The most common calculation asked with the Arrhenius equation is

options.text: Measuring the orders m and n
options.explanation: Orders come from rate experiments, not the Arrhenius line.

options.text: Balancing the equation of the reaction
options.explanation: Nothing here involves balancing.
Half-life belongs to order analysis.

options.text: Finding the activation energy from measured k and T values
options.explanation: That is the standard exam task of this topic.

questions.stem: In ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT), the constant ln A acts as

options.text: The intercept of the straight-line plot of ln k against 1/T
options.explanation: Setting 1/T to zero leaves ln k = ln A.
The gradient is -Ea/R.
That is Ea in the slope.
T sits in the x-variable 1/T.

questions.stem: A reaction's k is measured at two temperatures. To extract Ea, you should

options.text: Substitute the temperatures into the rate equation
options.explanation: The rate equation carries orders, not Ea.

options.text: Apply Ea = RT(ln A - ln k) using the known A, or plot ln k against 1/T and use the gradient
options.explanation: Both routes come straight from the log form.

options.text: Average the two k values and multiply by R
options.explanation: No averaging law exists here.
Squaring k has no basis in the equation.

questions.stem: Write the logarithmic form of the Arrhenius equation.
questions.modelAnswer: ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT), where each symbol keeps its Arrhenius meaning.

questions.stem: State the effect on k of raising temperature and of raising activation energy.
questions.modelAnswer: Raising temperature increases k; raising activation energy decreases k.

questions.stem: Explain why the logarithmic form is easier to use for calculations than the original exponential equation.
questions.modelAnswer: The log form is linear in the variables: ln k depends on 1/T through the single constant combination Ea/R, so an unknown such as Ea can be isolated and solved algebraically instead of un-doing an exponential.

questions.stem: A student computes Ea from two k-T pairs but reports it in J mol-1 while the mark scheme expects kJ mol-1. What went wrong and what is the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: Nothing is wrong except the unit presentation: with R = 8.31 J mol-1 K-1 the arithmetic returns joules, so the student should divide by 1000 to express the answer in kJ mol-1.

questions.stem: The gradient of a plot of ln k against 1/T equals

options.explanation: ln A is the intercept, not the gradient.
No such slope exists in the equation.
The slope of the Arrhenius straight line is the negative ratio of activation energy to gas constant.
The minus sign from the log form must not be dropped.

questions.stem: The intercept of the ln k versus 1/T line gives

options.explanation: Ea lives in the gradient.
Temperature is folded into 1/T.
R is a fixed universal value, not a graph feature.

options.text: ln A, from which A = e^(intercept)
options.explanation: Setting 1/T = 0 in the log form leaves ln k = ln A.

questions.stem: Before plotting, the experimental data must be transformed by

options.text: Taking ln of each k value and computing 1/T for each temperature
options.explanation: Those are exactly the plotted quantities.
No squaring rule exists in this method.
R belongs to the gradient, not the raw data.
Kelvin is required throughout.

questions.stem: A plotted Arrhenius line has gradient -1.0 x 10^4 K. With R = 8.31 J mol-1 K-1, Ea is about

options.text: Negative, because the gradient is negative
options.explanation: The minus sign is consumed by the definition; Ea is positive.

options.text: 8.3 x 10^4 J mol-1, since Ea = gradient magnitude x R
options.explanation: Multiplying 1.0e4 K by 8.31 J mol-1 K-1 gives about 8.3e4 J mol-1.

options.text: 1.2 x 10^-4 J mol-1, dividing R by the gradient
options.explanation: The operation is multiplication, not division.
The gradient magnitude carries the 10^4.

questions.stem: On an Arrhenius plot, points that curve away from a straight line indicate

options.text: That A varies enormously with temperature
options.explanation: A is treated as effectively constant.
Zero Ea would give a horizontal line, not curvature.

options.text: Data or handling errors, because the true relation is linear in these variables
options.explanation: The Arrhenius treatment predicts a line, so curvature signals a mistake.

options.text: A change in the reaction's orders
options.explanation: Orders never appear in the Arrhenius variables.

questions.stem: State the gradient and the intercept of the ln k against 1/T plot.
questions.modelAnswer: The gradient is -Ea/R and the intercept is ln A.

questions.stem: State the two conversions applied to raw k and T data before plotting.
questions.modelAnswer: Each rate constant is converted to ln k, and each temperature to the reciprocal 1/T.

questions.stem: Explain why the Arrhenius plot gives a straight line.
questions.modelAnswer: Taking logarithms removes the exponential, leaving ln k as a linear function of 1/T with fixed coefficients ln A and -Ea/R, so plotting one against the other must produce a straight line.

questions.stem: A student's plotted line has intercept 30.2. Report A and comment on its size.
questions.modelAnswer: A = e^(30.2), roughly 1.3 x 10^13, an enormous pre-exponential factor typical of gas-phase reactions where the steric factor multiplies collision frequency into a very large constant.
